questions.stem: A council is replacing the booking system used by its cemeteries and crematorium. Both the contract and the requirements document describe the replacement as like for like. In acceptance testing the bereavement services manager objects that clerks cannot hold a slot while a family decides. The old system never did this either; staff kept a pencil diary beside the screen. She says like for like means the whole way of working, not the software. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Add a slot-hold feature under the existing contract, since the working practice predates the project.
options.rationale: Concedes scope on the strength of whoever raises the objection most convincingly. It treats a newly surfaced expectation as an entitlement without ever establishing what the two parties agreed, which invites the same move on every subsequent finding.

options.text: Establish in writing what each party understood like for like to cover, then decide whether the hold sits inside or outside it.
options.rationale: The disagreement is about the meaning of an agreed phrase, so the meaning is what has to be settled before anything else can be. Written agreement on the boundary is what makes the next twenty findings cheap to resolve.

options.text: Point to the requirements document and confirm that the slot hold is outside the agreed scope.
options.rationale: Wins the contractual point and loses the user. The manager is not claiming the document says something it does not; she is claiming the document means something it does not, and quoting it back answers a question she did not ask.

options.text: Raise a change request for the slot hold and let the change control board rule on it.
options.rationale: Routes a definition dispute through a body that decides on changes to an agreed baseline. Nobody has yet established that the baseline covers this, so the board would be voting on an interpretation rather than a change.

questions.explanation: Words like equivalent, like for like and business as usual pass review because everyone reads them as their own expectation, and they only fail when something concrete tests them. When such a phrase is challenged, the work is to convert it into an explicit boundary agreed by both parties, rather than to concede or to cite. A shared word is not a shared expectation, and a project discovers the difference at the worst possible moment unless it goes looking earlier.
questions.mindset: Treat an agreeable phrase as an unresolved question until both sides have written down what it excludes.

questions.stem: Your squad builds the app for a city bike hire scheme. At a refinement session the transport authority's contract manager notices an item called cargo bike bookings sitting in the backlog. He tells you he is pleased it is coming and mentions he will let the cycling forum know at their meeting next week. The item has never been estimated, sized or prioritised against anything else. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain before he leaves that a backlog item is a candidate, not a commitment, and agree what he can safely tell the forum.
options.rationale: The expectation is about to be repeated to a third party, which is the moment it becomes expensive to correct. Settling the wording now costs a minute and saves an eventual retraction in front of an audience.

options.text: Prioritise the item into the next sprint so that the statement he intends to make becomes true.
options.rationale: Lets an offhand remark set the order of work ahead of everything the team has already weighed. Priority earned by who spoke last is how a backlog stops being a ranking of value and becomes a queue of the loudest requests.

options.text: Remove the item from the backlog so that it cannot be misread by other stakeholders.
options.rationale: Destroys a legitimate record of a possible future feature in order to prevent a misunderstanding. The backlog is not the problem; the assumption that presence implies delivery is, and hiding the list leaves that assumption intact.

options.text: Wait until the next review, when the increment will show what has actually been built.
options.rationale: Allows the statement to be made to the cycling forum first. Correcting an expectation after it has been passed on means correcting several people who never heard it from you, and each of them heard it as news.

questions.explanation: A backlog is a ranked list of things that might be done, and the ordering carries no promise about any of them. That is obvious to a team who see items rise and fall every fortnight and invisible to a stakeholder who sees a list of features with their name on. The moment to correct the reading is before it is repeated, because the cost of an expectation rises with every person who has heard it.
questions.mindset: Correct a misreading while it is still one person's, not after it has been passed on.

questions.stem: A regional theatre's new box office system goes live in nine weeks. The front of house manager has been planning her rotas on the basis that two of your developers will sit in the box office through the autumn season, as they did during the pilot fortnight. Your funding covers four weeks of post-live support, after which the team disbands. Nobody has ever written down how long support lasts. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell her the support period is four weeks and that this was always the funded position.
options.rationale: Accurate and useless. It closes the conversation with an assertion about the past instead of opening the one that matters, which is what her autumn actually needs and who will provide it.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to extend funding so the team can stay for the season, since the expectation has already been planned around.
options.rationale: Treats an unstated assumption as a requirement to be funded. It also removes her incentive to build the internal capability she will need in any case, because the answer to every gap becomes another extension.

options.text: Agree the support period explicitly now, work out what her autumn needs, and plan how those needs are met after week four.
options.rationale: Names the boundary and then does the work the boundary creates. Nine weeks is enough time to build the alternative, which is the only reason raising it now is better than raising it at go-live.

options.text: Keep the pilot arrangement informally, since two developers will still be in the organisation on other work.
options.rationale: Creates a support model that depends on goodwill and unbooked time, with nobody accountable for response. It fails silently on the first week both developers are committed elsewhere, which will be during her busiest season.

questions.explanation: Support after go-live is the expectation most often set by demonstration rather than agreement: people plan around the level of attention they experienced during a pilot, which was deliberately generous and temporary. The correction is not simply to state the funded period, because a stated boundary leaves the underlying need unmet and it will return as an escalation. Naming the boundary early is worth doing only because it creates time to build what sits on the other side of it.
questions.mindset: State a limit early enough that there is still time to build what has to replace it.

questions.stem: A marina asks you to scope a replacement berth management and billing system. Asked in a corridor for a rough figure, you said about £180,000, plus or minus thirty per cent, before any design work. Three weeks later the harbour master's board paper proposes the project at a cost of £180,000, with your name beside the number and no range. The paper goes to the board in five days. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask for the range and its basis to be restored in the paper before it goes to the board.
options.rationale: The board is about to approve a figure whose uncertainty has been stripped out. Restoring the range before approval costs an edit; restoring it after approval costs a change request and your credibility as the source of the number.

options.text: Let the paper stand and manage delivery to £180,000, treating the figure as the target to work within.
options.rationale: Accepts a commitment created by someone else's editing. Working to the optimistic end of an untested range means every subsequent honest estimate reads as an overrun rather than as information.

options.text: Ask for the figure to be raised to £234,000 so that the upper end of your range is the approved budget.
options.rationale: Swaps one point number for another and keeps the same flaw. It also spends contingency that has not been justified, and invites a challenge you cannot answer because no design work has been done.

options.text: Withdraw the estimate and tell the harbour master that no figure can be given until design is complete.
options.rationale: Refuses to inform a decision that will be taken with or without you. An early estimate with its uncertainty attached is more useful than silence, and silence is usually filled by somebody else's number.

questions.explanation: An estimate carries two pieces of information, the figure and its uncertainty, and only the figure survives being retold. The loss happens in ordinary summarising rather than in bad faith, which is why it has to be caught at each point the number is copied into a document that will be approved. Once a range is approved as a point, the range cannot be recovered without appearing to ask for more money.
questions.mindset: An estimate without its uncertainty attached has stopped being an estimate.

questions.stem: You have run a half-day session to align the auction team, the harbour office and the buyers' representatives on how a coastal fish market's new e-auction will handle late landings. The session ended warmly, everyone said they were happy, and you wrote the outcome up in a page that nobody has disputed in the week since. You have seen apparent agreement dissolve before. Which two actions best test whether this alignment is real?

options.text: Ask each group to describe, in their own words, what will happen to a boat landing forty minutes after the cut-off.
options.rationale: A shared abstraction survives a meeting; a shared answer to a specific case does not unless the alignment is genuine. Divergence shows up in the detail, which is exactly where the writing-up smoothed it over.

options.text: Ask each group what they have now stopped planning for, or changed, as a result of the agreement.
options.rationale: Agreement that has changed nobody's behaviour is agreement to end a meeting. A group that has altered a rota or a contract clause has acted on the decision, which is the only evidence that costs them something.

options.text: Circulate the write-up again and ask for written confirmation from each group.
options.rationale: Collects signatures on a document each party still reads in its own way. Confirmation of a text tests whether people object to the words, not whether they mean the same thing by them.

options.text: Add the agreement to the risk register so that any later divergence is visible.
options.rationale: Logs the possibility of failure instead of testing for it now, while it is cheap. The register is a record of things you are watching, and this is something you can settle this week.

options.text: Schedule a follow-up session in six weeks to revisit the agreement.
options.rationale: Defers the test past the point at which the three groups will have built six weeks of incompatible plans. The value of testing alignment is highest immediately, when correcting it is still just a conversation.

questions.explanation: The failure mode of an alignment session is that agreement on a principle is mistaken for agreement on its consequences, and warmth in the room is read as evidence. Two things distinguish real alignment: parties independently produce the same answer to a concrete case, and parties have changed something of their own because of it. Restating the words in more places tests neither, however many people confirm them.
questions.mindset: Test agreement by what people now do differently, not by whether they object to the write-up.

questions.stem: A coroner's service is replacing its case management system. The senior coroner has said throughout that the system must never leave a family without a named contact during a transfer of a case between officers. Your design routes transfers through a queue, with reassignment inside one working day. She has raised this three times and you have three times explained the queue. She has not accepted it. The build starts in a fortnight. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to have the design decision confirmed, so the build can start on schedule.
options.rationale: Uses authority to settle a question of substance. It may produce a decision, but it converts a stakeholder with a legitimate concern into someone who has been overruled, and she will be present at every acceptance gate.

options.text: Treat the repeated objection as evidence the requirement is real, and re-examine whether the design can meet it.
options.rationale: Three explanations that have not landed usually mean the explaining is not the problem. Reopening the design while it is still cheap is the response that takes her position seriously as information rather than as resistance.

options.text: Document the queue design as an accepted risk with her objection recorded, and proceed.
options.rationale: Converts an unresolved disagreement into paperwork. Recording that someone disagreed does not make the disagreement safe to build over; it merely establishes who will be quoted when it surfaces at acceptance.

options.text: Offer to review the queue behaviour after six months of live running, once real transfer volumes are known.
options.rationale: Defers a design question past the point where design can change. For a bereaved family, six months of the wrong behaviour is not a trial period, and she is unlikely to read the offer as anything but a refusal.

questions.explanation: Alignment is often taught as bringing a stakeholder to the plan, and the harder case is the one where the plan should move instead. A stakeholder who returns to the same point after being given a full explanation is usually not confused, and repetition from a credible source is evidence about the requirement rather than about the person. The judgement is whether the objection concerns something the project exists to protect, and if it does, the cheapest moment to act on it is always now.
questions.mindset: Ask whether a repeated objection means you have explained badly or designed wrongly.

questions.stem: On a county school transport routing programme, three stakeholders have each stated a firm expectation. Match each stated expectation to the underlying need it is actually expressing, so that you can look for an option that meets the need. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The finance lead insists the system must go live on the first day of the financial year and no later.
A head teacher insists on seeing every route change before it is published to parents.
The transport contractor insists on being given the full year's routes in one file, twelve weeks ahead.

options.text: A need to book driver and vehicle capacity before a competitor takes it
options.rationale: The contractor is not attached to a file format. The twelve weeks is a procurement lead time, and any commitment that lets capacity be booked that early will serve, including a partial or provisional route set.

options.text: A need to avoid a second set of parent complaints landing in the school office
options.rationale: The review request is a defence against being the visible face of an unexplained change. Advance notice, or a note explaining the reason, may meet it without giving one school a veto over publication.

options.text: A need to keep the cost in a single budget year rather than split across two
options.rationale: The date is a proxy for an accounting boundary. If the spend can be committed in the right year, the go-live date itself may have more room in it than the finance lead's phrasing suggests.

options.text: A need to be seen by peers as having influenced the programme
options.rationale: Not used. Status motives exist, but reading one into a stated expectation without evidence is a way of dismissing it. Each of these three has a checkable operational reason behind it, and assuming otherwise closes off the option you are looking for.

questions.explanation: A stated expectation is a solution somebody has already chosen, and it usually conceals the need that made them choose it. Working back to the need widens the set of acceptable answers, which is what makes alignment possible when the stated positions are incompatible. The discipline is to look for the operational reason first, because attributing a motive to someone forecloses the search and is difficult to recover from if you are wrong.
questions.mindset: Ask what a demand is for before deciding whether it can be met.

questions.stem: Your team builds a claims product for a pet insurer. The claims director has worked out that your team completes roughly forty points a sprint with eight people over ten days, and has started converting sizes herself. In a planning session she says a thirteen-point item is about three days of work and asks why an eight-pointer is scheduled across two sprints. She is not hostile; she thinks she has understood the system. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain what points measure and what they do not, and agree a different way to answer her scheduling questions.
options.rationale: She has a real question about when things arrive and has built the only model available to her. Replacing the model with something that answers the same question is what stops her rebuilding it next month.

options.text: Convert the team's estimates to days so that everyone is working in the same unit.
options.rationale: Solves the confusion by adopting it. Duration estimates per item invite the tracking of individual variances and lose the relative sizing that made the team's forecasts stable in the first place.

options.text: Ask her not to convert points, since sizing is the team's internal concern.
options.rationale: Declines to answer a legitimate stakeholder question and marks a shared forecast as private. She will keep converting, only now without correction and without telling you the answers she reaches.

options.text: Show her the sprint burndown so she can see the work completing at its actual rate.
options.rationale: Offers more of the same data to someone whose problem is the interpretation, not the supply. A burndown read through a points-equal-days model simply confirms the model on the sprints where it happens to fit.

questions.explanation: Relative sizing works because it deliberately discards duration, and a stakeholder outside the team has no way of knowing that a number which behaves like effort is not effort. Correcting the arithmetic is only half the job: the question underneath it, about when a particular thing will arrive, is legitimate and needs a channel of its own. An explanation that leaves the original question unanswered will be quietly replaced by whatever model the stakeholder can build unaided.
questions.mindset: When someone misuses your numbers, find out what question they were trying to answer with them.

questions.stem: A tyre-fitting chain piloted your new job-card system at three branches. During the pilot a systems analyst visited each branch weekly, fixed data problems the same day and rewrote two reports on request. The pilot is judged a success and the regional managers for the remaining twenty-seven branches have been told to expect the same rollout. You have one analyst and eleven weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out what the twenty-seven branches will actually receive, and agree the difference from the pilot with the regional managers before the rollout starts.
options.rationale: The pilot set an expectation nobody stated, and it can only be corrected before people plan around it. Naming the difference in advance turns an inevitable disappointment into an agreed service level.

options.text: Run the rollout as it stands and manage complaints from branches as they arise.
options.rationale: Chooses to discover the gap twenty-seven times rather than settle it once. Each branch experiences it as a personal downgrade, and the analyst spends the eleven weeks apologising rather than deploying.

options.text: Slow the rollout so that each branch can receive the pilot level of support from the single analyst.
options.rationale: Preserves the service by abandoning the timescale, without checking that anyone would trade one for the other. It also treats a support model designed for three sites as if it were the thing being rolled out.

options.text: Ask the pilot branches to support their neighbours, since they have already been through it.
options.rationale: Transfers a support obligation onto people who never agreed to it and have their own targets. Willingness in the first fortnight is not capacity across eleven weeks, and nobody is accountable when it lapses.

questions.explanation: A pilot is run under conditions chosen to remove obstacles, and everyone who watches it forms an expectation of the whole rollout from what they saw. The support intensity is the part that scales worst and is least likely to have been written down. Stating the real service level before the rollout begins costs one uncomfortable conversation, where discovering it site by site costs the same conversation many times over with less goodwill each time.
questions.mindset: Say which parts of a pilot were temporary before anyone plans on them continuing.

questions.stem: Your appointment scheduling product serves a chain of physiotherapy clinics. The signed agreement commits to 99.5 per cent availability in each thirty-day month. The clinics' operations manager has told her reception teams that the system will be, in her words, always on, and has withdrawn the paper fallback sheets from every site. You want to show her the size of the gap between what has been committed and what she has assumed, in units she can picture.

blanks.label: Permitted downtime in a thirty-day month at 99.5 per cent, in hours
blanks.rationale: A thirty-day month is 720 hours, and 0.5 per cent of 720 is 3.6 hours. That is the outage the agreement already permits without anything having gone wrong.

blanks.label: Permitted downtime in the same month at 99.9 per cent, in minutes
blanks.rationale: 0.1 per cent of 720 hours is 0.72 hours, which is 43.2 minutes. The half-percentage-point difference between the two figures is worth roughly three hours of reception time a month.

blanks.label: Name the artefact that should record the availability level both sides are held to
blanks.rationale: The committed level belongs in a service level agreement, which is the document operations plans against. A figure that lives only in a contract schedule the operations manager has never read will not change how she runs her reception desks.

questions.explanation: Availability figures are read as adjectives rather than as quantities, and two numbers that sound almost identical describe very different operational days. Converting a percentage into the hours somebody will spend without a system is what makes an expectation checkable, because it can then be compared against the fallback arrangements that actually exist. The commitment matters less than whether the people who depend on it have planned for the outage it permits.
questions.mindset: Turn a percentage into the hours someone will have to work around before calling it agreed.

questions.stem: You publish a Now, Next and Later roadmap for a farm machinery dealer network's parts portal. At a distributor forum, two dealers refer to a Next item as arriving in the autumn quarter and one has told a supplier so. Reviewing the roadmap page, you find that Now, Next and Later are the only labels and that the page has not changed for five months. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add explicit confidence and horizon wording to each band, and re-establish a cadence for updating the page.
options.rationale: Two faults produced this: the labels carried no statement of certainty, and a static page invited readers to supply their own timing. Fixing both is what stops the same inference being drawn again next quarter.

options.text: Add target dates to each roadmap item so that readers are not left to guess.
options.rationale: Answers a demand for certainty by manufacturing it. Dates on Later items are the least reliable thing the team knows and, once published, are the figures that will be quoted back when they move.

options.text: Correct the two dealers directly and ask them to pass the correction to the supplier.
options.rationale: Repairs one instance of a fault that the artefact will keep producing. Everyone else at the forum read the same page and left with the same impression, uncorrected.

options.text: Restrict the roadmap to an internal audience until the delivery sequence is firmer.
options.rationale: Removes the information rather than the ambiguity, and leaves dealers planning with nothing. Withdrawing a shared view tends to be read as evasion and it costs more trust than the original confusion did.

questions.explanation: A roadmap in ordered bands is a statement about sequence, and readers convert sequence into dates because sequence alone does not answer the question they came with. Two properties keep that conversion honest: each band carries an explicit statement of how firm it is, and the page visibly changes, since a document that never moves is read as settled. Publishing less is rarely the fix, because the expectation forms anyway and then forms without you.
questions.mindset: Say how firm each part of a plan is, or readers will decide for you.

questions.stem: A building society is moving its savings platform. The agreed migration scope is twenty-four months of transaction history, with older records left readable in an archive. Six weeks from cutover, the head of member services tells you her team has been told they will have everything, and she has briefed the contact centre that no member query will need the archive. The archive route takes about two minutes per query. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish how often the contact centre actually needs records older than twenty-four months, then agree the handling with her on that basis.
options.rationale: The disagreement is about a volume nobody has measured, and the answer changes what should be done. It converts a dispute about a promise into a decision about a workload, which is a question both of you can settle with evidence.

options.text: Extend the migration to cover the full history, since the contact centre has already been briefed.
options.rationale: Re-scopes a migration six weeks from cutover on the strength of a briefing you did not give. It also assumes the need is large without checking, which is the same error the briefing made.

options.text: Confirm the twenty-four month scope in writing and ask her to re-brief the contact centre.
options.rationale: Restates the agreement and hands her the job of disappointing her own team. It is correct about the baseline and silent about the operational problem she is now holding, which is what she will remember.

options.text: Demonstrate the archive route to the contact centre so they can see it is workable.
options.rationale: Presents a workaround as a solution before establishing how often it will be used. Two minutes is trivial for five queries a week and unacceptable for two hundred, and the demonstration does not distinguish the two cases.

questions.explanation: Where an expectation and a baseline differ, the useful question is usually not which is authorised but how much the difference actually costs in operation. Sizing the gap turns a contest between two accounts of what was agreed into a shared problem with a measurable answer, and it frequently shows that the argument was about a case that barely arises. Deciding either way before measuring commits real money or real goodwill to a guess.
questions.mindset: Measure the gap between what was agreed and what is assumed before arguing about which should win.

questions.stem: You run the batch record system programme at a medical device manufacturer. The notified body expects design evidence assembled progressively and reviewable at each stage. Your sponsor expects the iterative delivery she was promised, and has told the executive that evidence will be produced once the design settles. Both have stated their position to the programme board, in the same meeting, without either noticing the conflict. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Set out for both parties, in one document, what each currently expects and where the two are incompatible.
options.rationale: Neither party has yet seen the conflict, and each believes the board endorsed their version. Putting the incompatibility in one place is the minimum condition for anybody to make a decision about it.

options.text: Establish which evidence must be produced at each stage regardless of later design change, and build that into the iteration pattern.
options.rationale: Tests whether the conflict is real across its whole range. Much regulatory evidence concerns process rather than final design and can be produced early without rework, which shrinks the genuinely contested part to something decidable.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to accept the regulator's position, since regulatory requirements are not negotiable.
options.rationale: Treats the whole of an expectation as fixed because part of it is. It also skips the analysis that would show how much of the sponsor's approach actually survives, and so concedes more than the regulator asked for.

options.text: Ask the notified body to confirm its expectations in writing before raising the conflict internally.
options.rationale: Spends weeks converting a clear position into a formal one while the sponsor continues briefing the executive on the other version. It also invites the regulator to answer more conservatively than it would have informally.

options.text: Record the conflict as a risk and monitor it until the design approach is settled.
options.rationale: Files a known, present incompatibility as a possible future event. Monitoring changes nothing about a conflict where both parties are already acting on incompatible assumptions and telling other people so.

questions.explanation: The dangerous expectation conflicts are the ones where both parties think they have been heard, because each has been, separately. Surfacing the incompatibility explicitly is necessary but rarely sufficient, since a bare conflict invites a contest of authority. The work that makes it decidable is establishing how much of each position can be satisfied simultaneously, which usually leaves a much smaller genuine trade-off than the original statements implied.
questions.mindset: Before choosing between two expectations, find out how much of both can hold at once.

questions.stem: Three weeks after starting on a zoo's membership renewal system, your team shipped a working renewals page, having found an existing component that did most of the job. The commercial director has since described the team as fast in two meetings and has asked for the gift membership flow on a similar timescale. That work has no equivalent component and touches payment handling. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain why the first delivery was quick, and give a forecast for the gift flow on its own terms.
options.rationale: The director has generalised from one observation because nobody offered her the reason. Supplying the reason alongside a separate forecast is what stops the first result becoming the standard she measures everything against.

options.text: Accept the timescale and look for savings elsewhere in the sprint to protect it.
options.rationale: Buys approval now by committing to a date derived from an unrelated piece of work. When it slips, the credibility lost is not just this forecast's but that of the fast delivery that preceded it.

options.text: Point out that three weeks was exceptional and decline to give a date until the payment work is understood.
options.rationale: Correct about the exception and unhelpful about the need. She has commercial decisions to make and will assume a timescale in the absence of one, most likely the last one she saw.

options.text: Deliver a partial gift flow within three weeks so that the pace appears to be maintained.
options.rationale: Manages the appearance of pace at the cost of a half-finished payment path. It also confirms the very expectation that is causing the problem, making the next conversation harder than this one.

questions.explanation: An early win sets a rate in the observer's mind, and observers cannot see which part of the result came from the work and which from a lucky reuse. Left unexplained, one favourable data point becomes the baseline against which everything later is judged slow. The response is to attach the reason to the result at the moment it is celebrated, and to forecast each subsequent piece from its own characteristics rather than from the last outcome.
questions.mindset: Explain why something was fast, or the exception becomes the expectation.

questions.stem: You take over delivery of a gate control system for a rail freight terminal. The client's terminal manager keeps referring to weighbridge integration, which he says was demonstrated during the bid. It is not in the signed contract or the requirements schedule, and the two people who ran the bid have left your firm. He is not being difficult; he plainly believes it was agreed. Delivery is seven months. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what was shown at bid stage and why it did not reach the contract, then take the finding to him with an option.
options.rationale: Both accounts are currently guesses. Finding out what happened lets you separate an honest misunderstanding from an omission your own firm made, and the two situations deserve different offers.

options.text: Tell him the contract is the agreed record and that weighbridge integration is outside it.
options.rationale: Right about where obligations live and wrong about what the moment requires. It answers a sincere belief with a technicality, and the belief was probably created by your own organisation.

options.text: Absorb the integration into the delivery to preserve the relationship, and manage the impact quietly.
options.rationale: Concedes an unpriced scope item and hides its cost, which removes any chance of the client valuing the concession. It also sets the precedent that pre-contract recollections are honoured on request.

options.text: Ask him to produce written evidence that the integration was promised before considering it further.
options.rationale: Places the burden of proof on the party least able to discharge it and frames the exchange as a dispute. If the demonstration happened, the evidence sits in your firm's bid files rather than his.

questions.explanation: Expectations created before a contract is signed do not disappear when the contract omits them, and the people who created them are frequently gone. Establishing what actually happened comes first because it determines whether this is a gap in the client's understanding or a failure in your own handover from sales to delivery, and the fair response differs sharply between the two. Deciding before finding out means either conceding without cause or refusing without knowing.
questions.mindset: Find out how an expectation was formed before deciding who should carry the cost of it.

questions.stem: You have taken over a rail resignalling programme on which three agreed plans in a row were overturned within a fortnight of being settled. In each case somebody had said yes, and in each case the yes turned out not to bind anyone who mattered. You are now careful about what counts as agreement. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Someone who will be affected by a decision, but holds no authority over it, tells you informally that the plan looks fine to him. You should
The manager who holds the authority agrees a cutover plan that the night shift, who must carry it out, has never seen. You should
Two department heads each tell you privately that they accept the split of responsibilities, but neither will say so in the joint forum. You should

options.text: note it as a useful signal and still obtain agreement from whoever holds the decision
options.rationale: Acceptance from an affected party is worth having and cannot substitute for a decision. Treating it as one leaves the plan resting on somebody who was never in a position to commit to it.

options.text: test the plan with the people who must execute it before treating it as settled
options.rationale: Authority makes a decision binding, not workable. The people on the night will find the flaw regardless, and the only question is whether they find it before or after the plan is relied upon.

options.text: get the agreement stated in the shared forum before relying on it
options.rationale: Private agreement that nobody will repeat in public is usually agreement not to have the argument. Until it is said where both can hear it, each is free to remember it differently and neither has been contradicted.

options.text: ask the sponsor to rule on it so that the matter is closed
options.rationale: Not used. Escalation produces a decision without producing agreement, and each of these three situations already contains the ingredients of a real one. Spending sponsor authority here also makes it less available when something genuinely cannot be settled.

questions.explanation: An expectation counts as aligned only when the right person has agreed it, in a place where the agreement can be relied upon, with the people who must act on it having seen what they are agreeing to. Those are three separate tests and a plan can pass one while failing the others. Most collapses attributed to a change of mind are really cases where one of the three was never met and the gap went unnoticed because somebody said yes.
questions.mindset: Ask who agreed, where they said it, and whether the people doing the work have seen it.

questions.stem: Your team built a proof of concept that identifies species in camera trap images for a conservation trust. It runs on a laptop, has no access control, no error handling and a hard-coded model path. The trust's director watched it work on live footage and has told two funders the tool will be with field teams by the spring. She is genuinely enthusiastic and has repeated your team's own words back to you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out what stands between the demonstration and field use, with what each part needs, and re-agree the spring statement on that basis.
options.rationale: Makes the invisible work visible in terms she can weigh, which is what allows a commitment made to funders to be corrected with reasons rather than withdrawn. The correction is only credible if it is specific.

options.text: Harden the proof of concept for spring and defer access control and error handling to a later release.
options.rationale: Protects a date by deferring the parts that make the tool safe to leave with field teams. Deferring error handling in software that runs unattended in remote locations is deferring the failure, not the work.

options.text: Explain that a proof of concept is not a product and that spring is not realistic.
options.rationale: States a category and expects it to do the persuading. She has seen the thing work, which is stronger evidence to her than a distinction she has no reason to find meaningful.

options.text: Ask the trust's director to hold further statements to funders until a plan exists.
options.rationale: Sensible in isolation and insufficient, because the statement has already been made. It also puts the immediate cost on her while the information she needed to avoid the situation still has not been supplied.

questions.explanation: A prototype exists to answer one question and is built by deliberately omitting everything not needed to answer it, so the gap between working and usable is invisible to everyone who was not in the room when those omissions were chosen. Naming the category does not close that gap, because the observer's evidence is a working demonstration. What closes it is an itemised account of what remains, which lets someone who has made a public commitment revise it with a reason rather than an apology.
questions.mindset: When a demonstration has outrun the truth, itemise the difference rather than naming the category.

questions.stem: Your university estates decarbonisation programme reports by status colour to a board that meets monthly. Over two years no workstream has ever reported amber. You have learned that lead engineers believe amber triggers an intervention review, while the board believes amber simply means a lead wants help. Your boiler replacement stream should be amber this month. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Get the board and the leads to agree, in writing, what each colour means and what follows from it.
options.rationale: The colours have two definitions in circulation and neither group knows the other's. Until the meaning and the consequence are agreed by both, any individual report is being written in one language and read in another.

options.text: Report the boiler stream as amber this month with the reasoning attached, and say what response would help.
options.rationale: An agreed definition means nothing until somebody uses it and survives. Attaching the reasoning and the ask demonstrates the intended meaning in practice, which teaches the board more than the definition does.

options.text: Replace the colours with a numerical confidence score to remove the ambiguity.
options.rationale: Changes the notation while leaving the underlying problem, which is that nobody agreed what a signal obliges the board to do. A score of six will acquire its own folklore within two reporting cycles.

options.text: Report green with a written caveat in the commentary, since the board reads the commentary.
options.rationale: Preserves the record of unbroken green while hoping the caveat is noticed. It confirms to every lead that the colour is a political statement rather than a measurement, which is what produced two years of green.

options.text: Ask the leads to report honestly and assure them that no intervention review will follow.
options.rationale: Offers a personal assurance about how a board will behave, which is not yours to give. The first time a review does follow, the assurance is what the leads will remember and the reporting will close down further.

questions.explanation: A reporting scale is a shared language, and it fails quietly when the sender and receiver hold different accounts of what a signal obliges anyone to do. Agreeing the definitions is necessary but does not by itself change behaviour, because the existing behaviour is a rational response to a believed consequence. Belief changes when somebody sends the signal and the promised response actually occurs, which is why the definition and a demonstration of it have to travel together.
questions.mindset: A status signal means whatever people believe follows from it, not what the key says.

questions.stem: A city's air quality sensor network goes live in four months. Your design needs roughly two full-time posts to calibrate sensors, chase faults and publish the data. The environmental health manager who will own it after handover has been told the network is self-managing, and her budget submission for next year, already with the finance committee, carries no additional posts. She is not aware there is an issue. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out the running work the design creates, with what happens if it is not resourced, in time for her to amend the submission.
options.rationale: Her budget window is the binding constraint and it is about to close. Giving her the consequence as well as the requirement lets her argue for the posts or accept a reduced service knowingly.

options.text: Simplify the design so that the network genuinely requires no ongoing calibration.
options.rationale: Redesigns to fit an assumption nobody has tested, four months from go-live. Low-cost air quality sensors drift, so a design that needs no calibration is a design that publishes numbers nobody should rely on.

options.text: Raise the resourcing gap to the sponsor, since operating budgets sit outside the project's control.
options.rationale: Escalates past the person who holds the budget line and can still change it. It also arrives in her world as a decision taken about her department without her, which costs the working relationship at handover.

options.text: Include the calibration effort in the project's own budget for the first year to bridge the gap.
options.rationale: Postpones the problem by a year and conceals it in a closing project's costs. When the funding ends, the same conversation happens with less warning and with an established expectation that it was free.

questions.explanation: Projects are judged on delivery and handed to people judged on running cost, and the expectation that a new system is cheap to operate forms early and is rarely tested. The receiving manager's planning cycle, not the project's, sets the moment at which this can still be fixed cheaply. What has to be transferred is not just the requirement but the consequence of not meeting it, because that is what she needs in order to make the case or make an informed trade.
questions.mindset: Align the receiving manager's expectation of running cost while her budget can still move.

questions.stem: A care group is putting a new medication administration record onto tablets across fourteen homes. Four hundred and twenty care staff must be trained before go-live, which is eight weeks away. The training room holds fourteen people and the trainer can run three sessions a week. The operations director has told home managers that every member of staff will be trained before the tablets arrive. Work out the size of the gap before you go and see her.

blanks.label: Sessions needed to train all 420 staff
blanks.rationale: 420 divided by 14 per session is 30 sessions, assuming every session fills exactly. Any absence or repeat pushes the figure up, so 30 is the optimistic case rather than the expected one.

blanks.label: Weeks required at three sessions a week
blanks.rationale: 30 sessions at 3 a week is 10 weeks of continuous delivery with no trainer leave and no room clashes. It assumes the trainer does nothing else for the whole period.

blanks.label: Shortfall against the eight weeks available, in weeks
blanks.rationale: 10 weeks needed against 8 available leaves a 2 week shortfall, or about 84 staff untrained at go-live. That is the number the operations director needs, because it converts a broken promise into a decision about rooms, trainers or a staged start.

questions.explanation: A commitment about people being ready is a capacity calculation, and it is usually made before anyone does the arithmetic because the arithmetic looks trivial. Doing it converts a disagreement about whether a promise was wise into a decision with visible levers: more sessions a week, a larger room, a second trainer, or a rollout sequenced to match the training rate. Arriving with the size of the gap rather than the fact of it is what makes the conversation about options.
questions.mindset: Size a gap before raising it, so the conversation starts at what to do about it.

questions.stem: Your team builds parcel locker software for a courier network. At the quarterly review the operations director says the returns feature is not delivered. Your team released it to production five weeks ago and it works. Her depots cannot use it because the label stock they hold does not carry the new code, and no depot has been told the feature exists. Your team considers the item done and closed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with her what delivered will mean for the remaining features, and who is accountable for each part of getting there.
options.rationale: Both parties are using a word honestly and differently, and the gap will recur on every item until it is settled. Naming who owns label stock and depot communication is what prevents the same argument next quarter.

options.text: Take on depot communication and label stock ordering so that the feature becomes usable.
options.rationale: Fixes this instance by absorbing work the team is not resourced or placed to do. It also leaves the definition unresolved, so the team acquires an unbounded obligation on every future release.

options.text: Show her the release record confirming the feature went to production five weeks ago.
options.rationale: Proves a point about the team's obligation while conceding the one she is making. Nothing in the release record explains why a depot cannot process a return, which is the only fact she came with.

options.text: Extend the team's definition of done to include depot adoption for all future features.
options.rationale: Commits the team to a criterion it cannot control, since adoption depends on depot managers and procurement. A definition of done that includes other people's decisions makes the team's own signal meaningless.

questions.explanation: Delivered and usable are different claims, and each party naturally uses the word that matches what they are accountable for. The resolution is not for one definition to win but for the space between them to be mapped and assigned, because the work in that space is real and currently belongs to nobody. A team should not adopt a completion criterion that depends on decisions outside its control, and it should not pretend the remaining work does not exist.
questions.mindset: When two people use done differently, map the work between the definitions and give it an owner.

questions.stem: A cathedral is building a visitor centre. The head of the fabric advisory committee has begun returning drawings with instructions, and told a contractor last week that no stone specification proceeds without his approval. The governance approved by the chapter lists him as a consultee; approval sits with the chapter's project committee. He has forty years of expertise and is widely respected. The contractor now waits for him before ordering. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Speak to him first about what consultee means in practice here, and how his expertise will actually reach decisions, before anything is said to the contractor.
options.rationale: His expectation formed because consultation was never given a real shape, and correcting the contractor first would humiliate him into entrenchment. Offering a genuine route for his influence is what makes the boundary acceptable.

options.text: Write to the contractor confirming that only the project committee approves specifications.
options.rationale: Restores the correct process by correcting him in front of a third party. It is likely to convert a manageable overreach into a dispute at chapter level, where his standing is considerable and yours is not.

options.text: Ask the chapter to add him formally as an approver, since he is exercising the role in practice.
options.rationale: Amends governance to match whoever has taken authority. It also adds a second approval gate to every stone specification, which is a real schedule cost adopted to avoid one difficult conversation.

options.text: Let the arrangement continue while recording that decisions remain the project committee's.
options.rationale: Keeps the paperwork tidy while the actual decisions are taken elsewhere. When a specification is later challenged, the record will show an approval process that demonstrably was not followed.

questions.explanation: Expectations about authority are the ones people are least willing to have corrected in public, because the correction is heard as a statement about their standing. They usually form where a governance document names a role without describing what it entitles anyone to do. Correcting them therefore has two parts, and the order matters: settle it privately with the person first, and offer a real channel for the contribution, because a boundary that only takes influence away will be tested until it fails.
questions.mindset: Correct an expectation about authority in private, and offer somewhere for the influence to go.

questions.stem: An airline is replacing its crew training records system. Three expectations are currently unstated, and each has a point past which agreeing it becomes expensive. Match each expectation to the moment at which it must be settled. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: How much historic licence and check data will be visible in the new system rather than in an archive.
What response time crew planners will get during the Monday morning rostering peak.
How long the delivery team supports the crew office after go-live, and what it covers.

options.text: During requirements definition, because it sets the migration effort every other estimate depends on
options.rationale: History depth drives extraction, cleansing and reconciliation volumes. Settled late, it changes a figure that the schedule and the price have already been built on, so it moves everything.

options.text: When non-functional requirements are set before design, because the architecture is chosen to meet it
options.rationale: Performance under peak load is a property of the design rather than a feature added to it. Discovering the expectation after the architecture is fixed usually means rebuilding rather than tuning.

options.text: In the transition plan agreed before the go-live decision, because it commits people and money beyond the project
options.rationale: Post-live support spends resources that belong to the period after the project closes. It has to be agreed while there is still a decision to make about go-live, since afterwards the need exists whether or not anyone funded it.

options.text: At the closure review, where the project records what was delivered against what was agreed
options.rationale: Not used. Closure documents expectations that were settled earlier; it cannot settle them. Any of these three arriving first at closure means the project has already been run on three assumptions nobody checked.

questions.explanation: Every expectation has a last responsible moment, set by what depends on it rather than by how important it feels. Volume assumptions bind estimates, performance assumptions bind architecture, and support assumptions bind budgets outside the project. Working out what a given expectation constrains tells you when it has to be closed, and the ones that go unstated are almost always those nobody owns rather than those nobody has thought of.
questions.mindset: Fix the moment an expectation must be settled by asking what decisions depend on it.

questions.stem: Your team demonstrates a new case search for a legal aid provider using a seeded test set of about two thousand records. Results return instantly. The head of casework was impressed and has told her caseworkers that searching will no longer be something they wait for. The live estate holds around four hundred thousand cases across nine years, and the search has never been run against it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Test the search against a realistic data volume and share the result with her before her teams change how they work.
options.rationale: The expectation rests on a number nobody has yet produced. Getting the real figure is cheap now and settles whether there is anything to correct at all, which no amount of caveating would do.

options.text: Explain that demonstration environments are not indicative of production performance.
options.rationale: Offers a general caution in place of the specific fact. She has seen the search return instantly, and a disclaimer that produces no number leaves her with the only evidence she has.

options.text: Add an index and additional capacity now, since the live volume is clearly much larger.
options.rationale: Spends effort and money on a problem whose size is unknown. It may be unnecessary, and if the bottleneck is elsewhere it will not help while still having consumed the time available to find out.

options.text: Note the performance assumption in the risk register and review it before go-live.
options.rationale: Records something that can be answered this week as an uncertainty to be carried. Meanwhile her caseworkers are being told to plan around a behaviour that has never been observed.

questions.explanation: Demonstrations are built to show behaviour, not to measure it, and the conditions chosen to make the behaviour visible are exactly those that flatter performance. Where the resulting expectation is a quantity, the useful response is to produce the real quantity rather than to warn that the demonstration was unrepresentative. A caveat leaves the observer's evidence untouched; a measurement replaces it.
questions.mindset: Answer an expectation about a number by producing the number.

questions.stem: A gas distributor's meter replacement programme must move its completion date by five months, which you can evidence. Your two predecessors each moved it once, and each time announced a new firm date with confidence. Both moved again. The regional directors now plan on their own private estimates and one has said openly that programme dates mean nothing. You have to give the board a new date next week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Give the new date with the evidence behind it, the conditions under which it would move, and a named point at which it will be retested.
options.rationale: Two confident dates have already failed, so confidence is the one thing that carries no information here. Publishing the basis and the trigger conditions gives the directors something they can check for themselves, which is the only route back to being believed.

options.text: Add three months of buffer beyond the evidenced date so that this commitment is certain to hold.
options.rationale: Buys reliability with hidden padding that will be found. Once directors discover the margin, they will discount every future figure by an amount they guess, which is precisely the behaviour already damaging the programme.

options.text: Present the new date with an acknowledgement of the past failures and an assurance that this one is final.
options.rationale: Offers the same instrument that failed twice, with an apology attached. An assurance of finality is a claim about the future that nobody can evidence, and it is what the previous two announcements also contained.

options.text: Give a date range rather than a date, so that the uncertainty is visible to the board.
options.rationale: Honest about uncertainty and unusable for the board's purpose, which is to commit to regional resourcing. A range with no statement of what drives movement within it simply transfers the judgement to people with less information.

questions.explanation: Once dates from a source have failed repeatedly, the audience is no longer evaluating the date; they are evaluating the source, and any new number arrives already discounted. Restoring belief cannot be done by asserting more strongly, because assertion is what was discredited. It is done by changing the form of the commitment so it can be independently checked: the reasoning, the conditions that would break it, and a scheduled moment at which it is honestly retested.
questions.mindset: When your numbers have stopped being believed, publish what would change them rather than how sure you are.

questions.stem: You take over a vehicle auction platform programme. Two dealer groups have quoted a phase two capability set in recent correspondence, in wording taken from a slide deck your predecessor issued fourteen months ago. The scope changed nine months ago. The deck is still attached to the standard onboarding email that the commercial team sends every new dealer. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Find out what the two dealer groups have already committed to on the strength of it.
options.rationale: The document is the cause but the exposure is whatever they have promised their own customers or bought. Until that is known, you cannot tell whether this is a correction or a commercial problem.

options.text: Replace the attachment at its source in the onboarding email with a current, dated version.
options.rationale: The deck is not merely lying in an archive; it is being actively distributed to every new dealer. Correcting recipients while the pipeline keeps running means the same conversation with each new group indefinitely.

options.text: Email a correction to everyone on the deck's original distribution list.
options.rationale: Assumes the original list describes who holds the document, when it has been forwarded for fourteen months. It creates an appearance of thoroughness while missing most of the people who actually have it.

options.text: Ask the two dealer groups to disregard the phase two section of the deck.
options.rationale: Withdraws information without replacing it, leaving two commercial partners planning with a gap. It also gives them no way to work out what else in the deck is no longer true.

options.text: Mark the deck as superseded in the programme document library.
options.rationale: Corrects the copy that nobody outside the programme reads. Version control in the library has no effect on an attachment already circulating in an operational email template.

questions.explanation: A published artefact keeps setting expectations for as long as it circulates, and the copy under version control is rarely the one doing the damage. Two questions matter: where is it still being distributed from, and what have people already done on the strength of it. Correcting individual readers addresses neither, and a document withdrawn without a replacement leaves an information gap that people fill with the version they remember.
questions.mindset: Stop a stale document at the point it is being sent from, then find out what it has already caused.

questions.stem: Two contractors are upgrading ventilation and fire detection in a road tunnel. Both have agreed the systems will be fully integrated. In a design workshop it emerges that the ventilation contractor understands this as a shared alarm feed, while the detection contractor understands it as joint control logic with a single operator interface, which is roughly three times the work. Each cites the same clause. Detailed design closes in three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what the tunnel operator needs the two systems to do together, and specify the interface from that.
options.rationale: The clause cannot settle a dispute about its own meaning, so the operator's actual requirement is the only available arbiter. It also produces a specification that can be priced, which the phrase never could.

options.text: Take the more demanding interpretation, since it delivers the greater capability to the operator.
options.rationale: Buys capability nobody has yet shown is needed and hands one contractor a commercial claim for work outside its price. Choosing the larger reading of an ambiguous clause is not caution, it is an unpriced decision.

options.text: Take the lesser interpretation, since it is the common element both contractors accept.
options.rationale: Selects a scope by finding the overlap of two misunderstandings rather than by asking what the tunnel requires. Joint control logic may be a safety necessity, and the overlap has no bearing on that.

options.text: Refer the wording to the contracts team for a determination of what fully integrated means.
options.rationale: Asks for a legal reading of a phrase that has no settled technical meaning, and spends the three weeks waiting. A determination would establish liability without producing a design anyone can build.

questions.explanation: When two parties have signed the same words and read them differently, the words have stopped being useful evidence and arguing from them only hardens positions. The way out is to go behind the clause to the operational need it was meant to describe, and to specify from there. Choosing between the readings on any other basis, whether cautious or generous, commits money to an interpretation rather than to a requirement.
questions.mindset: When a shared clause has two readings, specify from the need it was written to serve.

questions.stem: At today's review of a leisure trust's swimming membership app, the marketing lead watched the family membership option being demonstrated. Afterwards she mentioned she has scheduled a post announcing it for Friday. The option is built but not released; three weeks of payment testing remain before it goes to customers. She is pleased and has already drafted the wording. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell her before she leaves that the option is not yet live, and agree an announcement date tied to the release.
options.rationale: The gap is between demonstrated and available, and she has no way to see it from the review. Correcting it before Friday costs a sentence; correcting it afterwards means members trying to buy something that does not exist.

options.text: Ask the team whether payment testing can be compressed so that Friday can be met.
options.rationale: Reshapes the delivery around a post that has not been discussed with anybody. Compressing testing on a payment path is where the compression is least affordable, and the date was never a requirement.

options.text: Ask her to postpone the post until the team confirms the option is ready.
options.rationale: Right about the postponement and vague about the replacement. Without a date she can plan a campaign around, she will either ask again next week or guess.

options.text: Let the post run and release the option as soon as testing allows.
options.rationale: Accepts a public announcement of something customers cannot buy. The complaints land on the trust's own reception staff, who were told nothing, and the app is what gets blamed.

questions.explanation: A review shows what a team has built, and observers reasonably read built as available because nothing in the demonstration marks the difference. The moment to close that gap is while the observer is still in the room, since the cost of an expectation rises sharply once it has been scheduled or published. Correcting it usefully means naming the real date, not merely withdrawing the wrong one.
questions.mindset: Say what is live and what is only built, before someone else says it for you.

questions.stem: A hospital group is consolidating laundry onto a single site. The business case claims a saving of £1,200,000 a year once the new site is running at full rate. The transition plan assumes no saving at all for the first three months after go-live, and then a saving rising evenly from nil to the full monthly rate across the following nine months. The finance director has put the whole £1,200,000 into next year's budget, starting at go-live.

blanks.label: Saving actually realised in the twelve months after go-live, in £
blanks.rationale: The full rate is £100,000 a month. Three months yield nothing, and a saving rising evenly from nil to £100,000 across nine months averages £50,000 a month, giving 9 × £50,000 = £450,000.

blanks.label: Amount by which next year's budget overstates the saving, in £
blanks.rationale: £1,200,000 budgeted against £450,000 realisable leaves £750,000 that has been committed elsewhere in the group's budget and will have to be found from somewhere else.

blanks.label: Name the artefact that should carry the agreed month-by-month phasing
blanks.rationale: A benefits realisation plan records when each benefit lands, not merely how large it is. Without it the annual figure from the business case is the only number anyone has, and it will be spent on the first day it becomes available.

questions.explanation: A business case states benefits at a steady-state annual rate, and everyone downstream reads that figure as available from the day the project finishes. The error is about timing rather than size, which makes it hard to spot: nobody has overstated the benefit, they have simply omitted the ramp. Phasing has to be agreed with whoever will book the saving, because the gap between rate and realisation falls entirely on their budget rather than on the project's.
questions.mindset: An agreed benefit is not aligned until both sides agree the month it starts arriving.

questions.stem: A wholesale florist is replacing its overnight ordering system. Deliveries arrive at two in the morning and orders are picked from three until six. The buying director has told her depot teams that the changeover will be seamless and that no ordering time will be lost. Your cutover plan needs a six-hour window with the system unavailable. She has not been consulted on the window. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Work out with her which six hours in the week cost the business least, and plan the cutover into that window.
options.rationale: The outage is not negotiable but its timing is, and she knows the trading pattern in a way you do not. Turning an unwelcome fact into a decision she makes is what converts opposition into a plan.

options.text: Explain that a changeover of this kind cannot be done without an outage.
options.rationale: States the constraint and stops. She now has a problem, no way to plan around it, and a briefing to her depot teams that she has to retract without being able to say what replaces it.

options.text: Run both systems in parallel for a week so that no ordering time is lost.
options.rationale: Buys the appearance of continuity at the price of double order entry through the busiest hours and a reconciliation problem afterwards. Parallel running is a serious commitment adopted here to avoid a conversation.

options.text: Assure her the outage will be kept as short as possible and manage the detail on the night.
options.rationale: Offers comfort in place of a figure. Deciding the window on the night means the depot teams find out when they arrive, which is exactly the outcome her briefing was trying to prevent.

questions.explanation: Some expectations cannot be met and the work is to find which part of them is genuinely fixed. Here the requirement is that trading is not disrupted, and the outage duration is a constraint while its placement is a choice. Handing the choice to the person who understands the operating rhythm produces a better window than you would pick, and it makes the constraint something they have shaped rather than something done to them.
questions.mindset: When you cannot remove a constraint, give the affected party the decision that is left.

questions.stem: A fertiliser plant is putting in a maintenance management system. Your plan needs four maintenance engineers for about a day and a half each per week over five months, to define asset hierarchies and job plans. The sponsor described this to the maintenance manager as a few workshops, and the manager's shutdown targets assume his engineers are unaffected. Nobody has done the arithmetic. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Put the demand in hours per engineer per week to the sponsor and the maintenance manager together, in one conversation.
options.rationale: The two hold incompatible pictures and have never compared them. A single figure discussed with both present prevents each hearing a version that suits them and prevents you carrying messages between them.

options.text: Establish which contributions genuinely need those four engineers and which could come from records or from other staff.
options.rationale: Reduces the ask to what only they can supply before asking for it. It is also the analysis that makes any refusal specific rather than a general objection to the project taking up time.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct the maintenance manager to release the engineers.
options.rationale: Uses authority to extract time from a manager measured on something the instruction ignores. Compliance under instruction typically arrives as the least useful engineer for the fewest hours that can be defended.

options.text: Reduce the requirement by building the asset hierarchy from existing maintenance records.
options.rationale: Adopts a solution before establishing whether the records are complete enough. On most plants they encode the errors of the last system, which is what the engineers were needed to correct.

options.text: Add the engineers' time to the plan and record the availability as a risk to be monitored.
options.rationale: Logs a known conflict between two stated positions as a possible future event. The shutdown targets and the plan are both live now, and monitoring will simply record which one gave way.

questions.explanation: The cost a project imposes on the business is the expectation least likely to be stated, because it never appears in the project's own budget. Aligning it means producing the figure in units the receiving manager plans in and putting it to both parties at once, since a demand relayed separately is heard as two different requests. Testing what only those people can supply is what makes the number defensible rather than merely large.
questions.mindset: State what a project will cost the business in the units the business plans in.

questions.stem: The chart tracks a national exam board's marking platform: a scope line, a completed work line, and a forecast fan drawn from the current status date. The launch date is fixed by the examination timetable and is marked on the chart. The board's chair has asked you for the single thing that tells her whether there is a problem she must act on. Select the gap you should put in front of her.

graphic.title: Burn-up chart with scope line, completed work and a forecast fan against a fixed launch date
graphic.caption: Select a gap. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Vertical gap between the scope line and completed work at the status date
regions.rationale: This is the work remaining, which tells her how much is left but nothing about whether it fits. A large remainder is fine with enough time and a small one is fatal without it, so the figure alone cannot support a decision.

regions.label: Horizontal gap between the fixed launch date and the earliest date the forecast reaches the scope line
regions.rationale: This is the shortfall that survives even the optimistic edge of the forecast, expressed in the unit the launch date is set in. It is the smallest true statement of the problem and the one that cannot be argued away by hoping for a good run.

regions.label: Vertical spread of the forecast fan where it crosses the launch date
regions.rationale: The fan width describes how uncertain the forecast is, not how far short it falls. Presented alone it invites the reply that the top of the range might yet be achieved, which is the conversation the chair does not need.

regions.label: Rise in the scope line between the start and the status date
regions.rationale: Scope growth explains how the position arose and is worth discussing later. It is a diagnosis rather than an exposure, and the chair asked what she must act on rather than who is responsible.

questions.explanation: A forecast against a fixed date has one figure that supports a decision: the distance between the date and the earliest completion the evidence allows. Quantities of remaining work, widths of uncertainty and histories of scope change all describe the situation without stating the exposure, and each invites a discussion that defers action. Choosing what to show is part of aligning an expectation, because the audience will act on whichever number they are given.
questions.mindset: Show the gap that holds even on the optimistic case, because that is the one that requires a decision.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the four places your free-flow tolling go-live date currently appears, with the value in each and who acts on it. The plan now supports November and the board pack is correct. Select the record that is currently causing money to be committed against a date the plan no longer supports.

graphic.title: Four records of a go-live date with their values and the party that acts on each
graphic.caption: Select a record. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between records, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Bid response — June — held by the client's procurement team
regions.rationale: Superseded at contract award and no longer acted on by anyone. A stale date in a closed bid file is untidy rather than expensive, because no decision downstream is taken from it.

regions.label: Signed contract — August — held by both parties' legal teams
regions.rationale: A genuine exposure that will need a formal change, but it commits no cash this week. Confusing a liability that must be corrected with a spend that is happening now leads to fixing the slower problem first.

regions.label: Operations resourcing plan — August — 40 agency toll staff booked and being inducted
regions.rationale: Agency staff are being paid and inducted against a date two revisions out of date, so every week of delay in correcting it is money that cannot be recovered. It is the only record here converting the error into irreversible cost.

regions.label: Latest board pack — November — held by the executive
regions.rationale: This one matches the plan and is the reference the others should be reconciled to. Selecting it treats the accurate record as the problem, which is what happens when records are audited for tidiness rather than for consequence.

questions.explanation: The same date lives in several records and they drift apart at different speeds, so correcting them all at once is rarely possible. Priority follows consequence rather than authority: the record to fix first is the one from which people are already spending money or committing resources, because that cost is accruing and cannot be recovered. Contractual and reputational corrections still have to happen, but they can be sequenced behind the one with an active meter running.
questions.mindset: Correct the version of the truth that people are spending money on first.

questions.stem: You are delivering asset tracking for a scaffolding hire company under a fixed price. The client's operations manager sends two or three small requests a week, each described as a tweak, and expects them included. Some are genuine clarifications of agreed requirements; others are new behaviour. Your team has absorbed eleven of them and is now behind. She has never been told there is a distinction.
