What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with her how the two kinds of request will be told apart, and what route each takes, before the next batch arrives.
options.rationale: She cannot apply a distinction nobody has explained, and eleven absorbed requests have taught her there is none. Agreeing the test together is what makes the first refusal land as a rule rather than as a change of attitude.

options.text: Keep absorbing the smaller requests and price only the substantial ones.
options.rationale: Leaves the boundary undefined and moving, which guarantees the argument happens later over an item on the wrong side of a line she has never seen. It also rewards splitting a request into smaller pieces.

options.text: Refer all further requests to the change process and point to the fixed price.
options.rationale: Treats clarifications of agreed scope as changes, which is both wrong and slow. It also reverses eleven weeks of practice without explanation, which she will experience as a hardening of position.

options.text: Log the requests and present the cumulative impact at the next monthly review.
options.rationale: Saves up a bill for work already done and delivered. Presenting the total after the fact removes any chance she had of choosing differently, which is the part she will object to.

questions.explanation: Where a boundary has never been stated, behaviour states it, and consistently absorbing requests establishes that everything small is free. Recovering from that is not a matter of enforcing the contract but of agreeing an explicit and mutual test for which side of the line something falls on. A test agreed in advance is applied to a category; a test introduced with the first refusal is heard as being applied to a person.
questions.mindset: Agree where a line sits before you need to hold it, or your first refusal defines you rather than the line.

questions.stem: Three statements were signed off in the summary for an audiology service's hearing aid stock product, and each is now being read differently by the clinical and supplier teams. Match each statement to the question that would make it testable. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Stock levels will be visible in real time.
The system will be easy for reception staff to use.
Reporting will cover the whole service.

options.text: Within how many minutes of a dispense must the count change, and at which sites?
options.rationale: Real time means anything from instant to overnight depending on who is speaking. A stated lag and a stated scope turn it into something a test can pass or fail, and something an architecture can be chosen for.

options.text: Which task, performed by whom, must be completed in what time without prior training?
options.rationale: Ease is a judgement until it is tied to a named person doing a named task to a stated standard. That form can be observed on a real reception desk, which no amount of discussion about usability can.

options.text: Which clinics, which product lines and which periods must a single report cover?
options.rationale: Whole service is exactly the word each department fills with its own boundaries. Listing the dimensions a report must span converts a shared word into an inventory that both teams can check.

options.text: How satisfied must users report being with the system in the survey after launch?
options.rationale: Not used. It replaces one vague statement with another and measures it after the point at which anything could be changed. A satisfaction target tells a designer nothing about what to build.

questions.explanation: Agreeable phrases survive sign-off precisely because each reader supplies their own meaning, and the divergence only appears when something concrete has to be accepted or rejected. Making such a phrase testable means asking for the threshold, the actor and the scope, since those are the dimensions on which readings differ. A restatement that is still unmeasurable, or measurable only after delivery, has moved the problem rather than solved it.
questions.mindset: Convert an agreeable phrase into a threshold, an actor and a boundary, or expect to argue about it at acceptance.

questions.stem: You are starting a peat restoration programme funded jointly by a water company, a wildlife trust and two landowners. None has worked with the others before and each has a different reason for taking part. You have a two-day inception meeting and want to reduce the chance of expectation gaps opening over the three years of the programme. What is the most useful thing to establish in that meeting?

options.text: How expectations will be recorded, reviewed and changed as the programme runs, and who does each.
options.rationale: Three years will invalidate whatever is agreed this week, so the durable asset is the mechanism rather than the content. It also gives partners a legitimate route to raise a change instead of quietly working to their own version.

options.text: A detailed statement of what each partner expects from the programme, agreed and signed at the meeting.
options.rationale: Captures the position on day one and preserves it as it goes stale. Without a route for updating it, the signed statement becomes the thing partners are compared against rather than the thing that keeps them aligned.

options.text: A shared set of objectives and measures that all four partners can commit to.
options.rationale: Necessary and not sufficient, and often achieved by choosing wording general enough for everyone to accept. Agreed objectives are where the expectation gaps hide rather than where they are prevented.

options.text: The governance terms of reference, meeting cadence and escalation route for the programme.
options.rationale: Establishes where decisions are taken without establishing how differences of expectation reach those decisions. Governance handles matters that have been raised, and the ones that damage a partnership are the ones nobody raises.

questions.explanation: On a long programme with unfamiliar partners, any set of expectations agreed at the start will be out of date well before delivery, and the work of alignment is continuous rather than initial. What survives is the mechanism: an agreed place where expectations are written, an agreed rhythm for revisiting them, and named people responsible. Setting that up at the point when everyone is willing costs a session, and it is much harder to introduce later once someone has been disappointed.
questions.mindset: Set up how expectations will be kept current, not just what they are today.

questions.stem: Your squad of seven works on a campsite booking product and also maintains a sister product for the same operator. Two product owners direct that work. Reviewing the last quarter you find each has been planning their roadmap on the assumption of the squad's full capacity, and neither knows the other exists on the team's board. Both are so far satisfied, because their highest priorities happened to be small. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Show both owners the actual split of the squad's time and get them to agree the allocation between them.
options.rationale: The information gap is the whole problem, and it is currently masked by luck. Agreeing an allocation between the two of them keeps the trade in the hands of the people entitled to make it rather than in the team's sprint planning.

options.text: Wait until a genuine clash occurs, then bring the two owners together with a concrete example.
options.rationale: Chooses to have the conversation at the worst moment, when one owner must lose something specific. A concrete example makes the discussion vivid and also makes it a contest rather than a design.

options.text: Ask the team to protect a fixed share of each sprint for the sister product.
options.rationale: Has the team set an allocation that neither owner has agreed to and neither knows about. It also makes the squad the party refusing work, which is a decision they have no authority to defend.

options.text: Ask the operator to fund a second squad so that each product has its own team.
options.rationale: Proposes a costly structural fix before anyone has established what the split should even be. It also skips the possibility that the current allocation is fine once it is visible and agreed.

questions.explanation: Where one team serves two demands, the allocation exists whether or not anyone has decided it, and in the absence of a decision the team makes it implicitly every sprint. Periods of apparent contentment are not evidence of alignment; they are evidence that the priorities have not yet collided. Surfacing the split while both parties are still satisfied lets them negotiate a rule, which is a very different conversation from arbitrating a clash.
questions.mindset: Surface a hidden trade-off while everyone is still happy, because that is when it can be agreed rather than arbitrated.

questions.stem: Your squad builds telematics for a plant hire firm. In the past fortnight three stakeholders have each asked for something the team cannot simply go and deliver, and each request is blocked for a different reason. You want to answer each one in the way its own obstacle calls for, rather than sending all three down the same route. Complete each sentence with the first move that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A stakeholder expects something the team could build, but only by displacing work she has previously said matters more. Your first move is to
A stakeholder expects a level of service the product cannot reach at any cost anyone would approve. Your first move is to
A stakeholder expects an outcome that is achievable, but only if her own department makes a decision it has been deferring. Your first move is to

options.text: show her the exchange and let her choose which of the two she would rather have
options.rationale: The constraint is capacity, not merit, and she is the person entitled to rank her own priorities. Presenting it as a choice keeps the decision with her and stops the team appearing to have quietly demoted her request.

options.text: say so plainly, with what is achievable, before she plans further around it
options.rationale: Nothing is gained by delay when the answer will not improve, and every week she plans around it increases the cost of the correction. Pairing the refusal with the achievable figure gives her something to replan with.

options.text: make the dependency explicit and agree who will take that decision by when
options.rationale: The expectation is reasonable and its owner is holding the blocker without realising it. Naming the decision and its date converts a disappointment waiting to happen into an action with somebody's name on it.

options.text: record it as outside the current scope and refer her to the change process
options.rationale: Not used. It answers three different situations with the same administrative move, and in each case the process would receive a request that the conversation should have resolved or reshaped first.

questions.explanation: An expectation that cannot be met as stated fails for different reasons, and the reason determines the response. A capacity conflict is a choice that belongs to the stakeholder; a genuine impossibility is information to be delivered early and paired with the achievable alternative; a blocked dependency is an action to be assigned. Routing all three into a process is what makes a project feel bureaucratic while leaving the underlying misalignment untouched.
questions.mindset: Diagnose why an expectation cannot be met before deciding how to answer it.

questions.stem: You committed a completion date for a vaccine cold store expansion to the health authority four months ago and have reported it as achievable since. Your commissioning lead told you twice early on that it could not be done, was not persuaded by your reasoning, and has stopped raising it. The team now works to a private date eleven weeks later, which you have seen in their own sequencing notes. The authority's next checkpoint is in three weeks. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Have the team produce its forecast openly, with its basis, so that the two positions can be compared as evidence rather than as opinions.
options.rationale: There are currently two dates and no shared analysis, and yours is the one being reported. Making the team's basis explicit is the only way to establish which is right, and it tests your own position as much as theirs.

options.text: Take the reconciled position to whoever holds the commitment to the authority, with options, before the checkpoint.
options.rationale: Three weeks is enough to revise a commitment deliberately and not enough to do it after the checkpoint has passed. Arriving with options rather than only a slippage keeps it a decision rather than a confession.

options.text: Reassure the commissioning lead that the reported date is a stretch target and that the real plan is understood.
options.rationale: Legitimises two operating dates and asks the team to keep the discrepancy. It also confirms that reporting is performative, which is why the lead stopped raising the issue in the first place.

options.text: Meet the workstream leads individually to understand their concerns before taking any position.
options.rationale: Reasonable early on and too slow now, with the checkpoint three weeks out. Individual conversations also let each lead calibrate to what they think you want, which is how the eleven-week gap survived unspoken.

options.text: Hold the committed date and add commissioning resource to close the eleven-week gap.
options.rationale: Commits money to defend a date before establishing whether the constraint is one that more people can relieve. Commissioning sequences are frequently limited by test durations and validation windows that added staff do not shorten.

questions.explanation: The most damaging expectation gap is often the internal one, because a team that has been overruled twice stops arguing and starts planning around you, and the project then runs on two dates with only one of them reported. Recovery requires making both forecasts and their reasoning visible so the disagreement becomes checkable, and then revising the external commitment deliberately rather than letting it be overtaken. A commitment nobody delivering it believes is not a commitment; it is a date the organisation has agreed not to discuss.
questions.mindset: If the people doing the work are planning to a different date, that is your date until you can show otherwise.

questions.stem: Your product now schedules collections for a waste oil recycler. For nine years their previous supplier gave the depot manager a named engineer's mobile number, and he used it perhaps twice a month. Your model is a shared queue with a four-hour response. He has escalated twice, saying the service has gone backwards, and both times the queue met its target. He is a well-liked and influential customer. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Find out what the old arrangement actually gave him, and design a way to deliver that inside your model.
options.rationale: Nine years of a named contact bought something specific, most likely someone who knew his depot and could decide without escalation. A queue can be made to supply site knowledge and decision authority, but only once you know which of them he is missing.

options.text: Assign him a named engineer, since the relationship matters more than the consistency of the support model.
options.rationale: Recreates the key-person dependency the shared queue exists to remove, and does it for the customer most likely to be copied by others. It also fails the first week that engineer is on leave.

options.text: Show him the response data demonstrating that the queue has met its target on both occasions.
options.rationale: Answers a complaint about the quality of the interaction with a measurement of its speed. He is not disputing the four hours; he is describing what happens inside them, and the data confirms his sense of not being heard.

options.text: Explain that the shared queue is standard and that the previous arrangement is not one you can offer.
options.rationale: Defends an internal operating decision to a customer who has no reason to care about it. It converts a solvable service design question into a statement that his experience is not going to improve.

questions.explanation: An expectation set by an incumbent is a description of an outcome, not a preference for a mechanism, and customers describe it in terms of the mechanism because that is what they saw. Copying the mechanism usually imports the weakness that made it worth replacing; dismissing it ignores a real need that was being met. The work is to identify which underlying property the old arrangement supplied, then to find where that property can live in the new model.
questions.mindset: When a customer asks for the old arrangement, work out what it gave them before deciding whether to recreate it.
